# Finish ANCOVA: Combining Regression and ANOVA {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## ANCOVA Review {.smaller}

Last week we introduced **Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)**, which combines:

-   **Continuous predictor** (covariate) — like body mass or temperature
-   **Categorical predictor** (factor) — like species or treatment

This week we continue with the biological motivations, interpretation, and assumptions.

## ANCOVA: Brain Size and Body Mass {.smaller}

![](images/week10_11_neanderthal_human_brain_size.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: Neanderthal vs. Modern Human {.smaller}

![](images/week10_12_neanderthal_human_skulls_skeletons.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: Brain-Body Mass Regression {.smaller}

![](images/week10_13_ancova_brain_body_mass_regression.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: ANOVA vs. Covariate Adjustment {.smaller}

![](images/week10_14_ancova_anova_vs_covariate_comparison.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: Adjusted Means {.smaller}

![](images/week10_15_ancova_adjusted_means_diagram.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

The key insight: by **adjusting for the covariate**, we can compare groups at the same value of the continuous predictor, removing confounding variation.

## ANCOVA: Multiple Covariates {.smaller}

![](images/week10_16_ancova_multiple_covariates_formula.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: Null Hypotheses {.smaller}

![](images/week10_17_ancova_null_hypotheses.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## ANCOVA: F-Ratio Table and Collinearity {.smaller}

![](images/week10_18_ancova_f_ratio_table.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

::: callout-warning
## Collinearity in ANCOVA

If the covariate and the factor are correlated (e.g., body mass differs between species), the order in which terms enter the model matters. Use **Type II or Type III sums of squares** from the `car` package to handle this properly.
:::

## ANCOVA: Heterogeneous Slopes {.smaller}

![](images/week10_19_ancova_heterogeneous_slopes.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

When slopes differ between groups, the interaction between the covariate and the factor is significant — this is a violation of the **parallel slopes assumption**.

## Parallel Slopes (Additive) Model {.smaller}

When there is no interaction, each group has the **same slope** but **different intercepts**:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i$$

### LaTeX

``` text
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{continuous} + \beta_2 x_{categorical} + \epsilon_i
```
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Parallel slopes model (additive)
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var, data = mydata)
```

-   The `+` means "additive" — the effect of the covariate is the same in every group
-   This produces parallel regression lines

## Interaction Model {.smaller}

When the relationship **differs between groups**, add an **interaction term**:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i$$

### LaTeX

``` text
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 (x_1 \times x_2) + \epsilon_i
```
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Model with interaction (different slopes)
lm(response ~ continuous_var * factor_var, data = mydata)

# Equivalent to:
lm(response ~ continuous_var + factor_var + continuous_var:factor_var,
   data = mydata)
```

## Interpreting ANCOVA Output {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Example with crickets data
lm(rate ~ temp + species, data = crickets)

# Output interpretation:
# (Intercept)      - baseline intercept for reference level
# temp             - slope (same for all groups)
# speciesO.niveus  - difference in intercept from reference
```

### Interpretation

-   The categorical variable coefficient represents the **offset from the reference group**
-   This is the same dummy variable encoding that `lm()` uses for ANOVA
-   The only difference from pure ANOVA is the inclusion of a continuous predictor
:::

## Parallel vs. Interaction: When to Use {.smaller}

| Model | Use When | R Formula |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Parallel Slopes** | Effect of covariate is same across groups | `y ~ x + group` |
| **Interaction** | Effect of covariate differs by group | `y ~ x * group` |

::: callout-tip
Always start with the interaction model. Test whether the interaction term is significant. If not, drop it and use the simpler parallel slopes model (parsimony principle).
:::

## ANCOVA: Type II/III Sums of Squares {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(car)

# Type II SS — tests each term after adjusting for all others
# (appropriate when no significant interaction)
Anova(lm(y ~ covariate + factor, data = mydata), type = "II")

# Type III SS — tests each term after adjusting for all others
# including interaction (appropriate when interaction is present)
Anova(lm(y ~ covariate * factor, data = mydata), type = "III")
```

### When to Use

| SS Type      | Use When                        | Notes                       |
|:-------------|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| **Type I**   | Balanced designs, order matters | Default in `anova()`        |
| **Type II**  | Unbalanced, no interaction      | Default in `car::Anova()`   |
| **Type III** | Unbalanced, interaction present | Requires `contr.sum` coding |
:::

## Visualizing ANCOVA Models {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: ancova-viz-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

# Simulated data for two groups
set.seed(42)
x <- rep(seq(1, 10, length.out = 20), 2)
group <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = 20)
y <- ifelse(group == "A", 2 + 0.8*x, 5 + 0.8*x) + rnorm(40, 0, 0.8)
df <- data.frame(x, y, group)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Parallel slopes
plot(x, y, col = ifelse(group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19,
     main = "Parallel Slopes Model")
abline(2, 0.8, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(5, 0.8, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Group A", "Group B"), col = c("steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19)

# Interaction model
set.seed(43)
y2 <- ifelse(group == "A", 2 + 0.5*x, 5 + 1.2*x) + rnorm(40, 0, 0.8)
plot(x, y2, col = ifelse(group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19,
     main = "Interaction Model (Different Slopes)")
abline(2, 0.5, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(5, 1.2, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Group A", "Group B"), col = c("steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: ancova-viz-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Parallel slopes
plot(x, y, col = ifelse(group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19,
     main = "Parallel Slopes Model")
abline(2, 0.8, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(5, 0.8, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Group A", "Group B"),
       col = c("steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19)

# Interaction model (different slopes)
plot(x, y2, col = ifelse(group == "A", "steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19,
     main = "Interaction Model (Different Slopes)")
abline(2, 0.5, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
abline(5, 1.2, col = "coral", lwd = 2)
```
:::

## Dangers of Extrapolation {.smaller}

All regression models (including ANCOVA) are only valid **within the range of the observed data**:

-   Polynomial models are especially dangerous to extrapolate — they can produce wildly unrealistic predictions outside the data range
-   Even linear ANCOVA predictions become unreliable far from the observed covariate values
-   Always report the range of your covariates alongside your model

::: callout-warning
## Rule of Thumb

Never predict beyond the range of your observed data unless you have strong theoretical justification for the extrapolation.
:::

# Multiple Linear Regression {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why Multiple Regression? {.smaller}

Multiple linear regression extends simple regression to include **two or more predictor variables**. The goals are:

-   Develop a better **predictive model** than possible from models based on single independent variables
-   Investigate the **relative individual effects** of each predictor variable above and beyond the effects of the other variables
-   The individual effects of each predictor on the response can be depicted by **partial regression lines**
-   The slope of any partial regression line represents the rate of change of that predictor on the response, **holding all other predictors constant** at their means

## Additive and Multiplicative Models {.smaller}

**Additive model** — each predictor contributes independently:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i$$

### LaTeX

``` text
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots + \beta_j x_{ij} + \epsilon_i
```
:::

**Multiplicative model** — includes an interaction between two predictors:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i$$

### LaTeX

``` text
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i
```
:::

## Additive vs. Multiplicative Models {.smaller}

![](images/week07_24_additive_vs_multiplicative_models.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## R Example: Multiple Regression with 2 Predictors {.smaller}

Read in the RNAseq_lip.tsv and examine whether Gene01 and/or Gene02 expression levels influence lipid content.

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

RNAseq_Data <- read.table('RNAseq_lip.tsv', header = TRUE, sep = '\t')

y  <- RNAseq_Data$Lipid_Conc
g1 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene01
g2 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene02

# Multiplicative model (with interaction)
Mult_lm <- lm(y ~ g1 * g2)
summary(Mult_lm)
```

### Questions

-   What are the parameter estimates of interest?
-   What are the outcomes from the hypothesis tests?
-   What happens when you remove the interaction term?
:::

## Additive Model Comparison {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Additive model (no interaction)
Add_lm <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2)
summary(Add_lm)
```

### Questions

-   Did any of the coefficient estimates change? Why?
-   Did the degrees of freedom change? Why?
-   Try different combinations of genes as predictors
:::

## Multiple Regression Assumptions {.smaller}

Multiple regression carries all the assumptions of simple regression plus an additional one:

1.  **Linearity** — the relationship between predictors and response is linear
2.  **Normality** — residuals are normally distributed
3.  **Homogeneity of variance** — constant variance of residuals
4.  **Independence** — observations are independent
5.  **No multicollinearity** — a predictor variable must not be strongly correlated with the combination of other predictor variables

::: callout-warning
## Multicollinearity

When predictors are highly correlated, coefficient estimates become unstable, standard errors inflate, and interpretation becomes unreliable. Always check for collinearity before interpreting a multiple regression model.
:::

## Checking for Multicollinearity {.smaller}

![](images/week07_25_multicollinearity_scatterplot_matrix.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(car)

# Visual check with scatterplot matrix
scatterplotMatrix(~ var1 + var2 + var3, diag = "boxplot")

# Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
model <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
vif(model)

# Tolerance = 1/VIF (values < 0.1 indicate severe collinearity)
1 / vif(model)
```

### Interpretation

| VIF Value | Interpretation                  |
|:----------|:--------------------------------|
| 1         | No collinearity                 |
| 1–5       | Moderate (usually acceptable)   |
| 5–10      | High (investigate further)      |
| \> 10     | Severe (remedial action needed) |
:::

## R Example: Three-Variable Regression {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

RNAseq_Data <- read.table('RNAseq_lip.tsv', header = TRUE, sep = '\t')
y  <- RNAseq_Data$Lipid_Conc
g1 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene01
g2 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene02
g3 <- RNAseq_Data$Gene03

# Three-predictor model
RNAseq3_lm <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
summary(RNAseq3_lm)
plot(RNAseq3_lm)

# Scatterplot matrices
library(car)
scatterplotMatrix(~ g1 + g2 + g3, diag = "boxplot")
scatterplotMatrix(~ y + g1 + g2 + g3, diag = "boxplot")

# Tolerance calculations (1 - R²)
1 / vif(lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3))
```

### Questions

-   Is there any evidence for multicollinearity?
-   Try running a simple regression of `y ~ g3` alone — how does the slope estimate for Gene03 compare to the partial slope estimate from the full model?
-   What does a change in slope estimate tell you about confounding?
:::

## Bioengineering Example: Scaffold Properties and Tissue Growth {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Simulated bioengineering data: predicting tissue growth
# from scaffold porosity, stiffness, and cell seeding density
set.seed(42)
n <- 60

scaffold_data <- data.frame(
  porosity     = runif(n, 40, 90),         # percent porosity
  stiffness    = runif(n, 5, 50),          # kPa
  seeding_dens = runif(n, 1e4, 1e6)        # cells/mL
)
scaffold_data$tissue_growth <- with(scaffold_data,
  0.8 * porosity + 0.3 * stiffness - 0.00001 * seeding_dens +
  0.005 * porosity * stiffness + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
)

# Fit multiple regression
scaffold_lm <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity + stiffness + seeding_dens,
                   data = scaffold_data)
summary(scaffold_lm)
```

### Questions

-   Which scaffold properties significantly predict tissue growth?
-   Does adding the interaction `porosity:stiffness` improve the model?
-   What happens to the seeding density coefficient when you remove it?
:::

## Diagnostic Plots for Multiple Regression {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: diag-plots-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
scaffold_data <- data.frame(
  porosity     = runif(n, 40, 90),
  stiffness    = runif(n, 5, 50),
  seeding_dens = runif(n, 1e4, 1e6)
)
scaffold_data$tissue_growth <- with(scaffold_data,
  0.8 * porosity + 0.3 * stiffness - 0.00001 * seeding_dens +
  0.005 * porosity * stiffness + rnorm(n, 0, 8))

scaffold_lm <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity + stiffness + seeding_dens,
                   data = scaffold_data)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(scaffold_lm)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: diag-plots-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Standard diagnostic plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(scaffold_lm)

# Using ggfortify for prettier diagnostics
library(ggfortify)
autoplot(scaffold_lm, which = 1:4) + theme_minimal()

# Cook's distance — identify influential observations
cooks_d <- cooks.distance(scaffold_lm)
plot(cooks_d, type = "h", main = "Cook's Distance",
     ylab = "Cook's Distance", xlab = "Observation")
abline(h = 4 / n, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

### Interpretation

-   **Residuals vs Fitted**: look for non-linearity (curved pattern) or heteroscedasticity (funnel shape)
-   **Q-Q Plot**: points should follow the diagonal line; deviations indicate non-normality
-   **Scale-Location**: check for constant variance (flat trend line)
-   **Residuals vs Leverage**: Cook's distance \> 4/n flags influential points
:::

## Partial Regression Plots {.smaller}

Partial regression (added-variable) plots show the effect of each predictor **after adjusting for all others**:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: avplots-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

library(car)
avPlots(scaffold_lm, main = "Added-Variable Plots")
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: avplots-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(car)

# Added-variable plots (partial regression plots)
avPlots(scaffold_lm)

# Each plot shows the relationship between one predictor
# and the response, holding all other predictors constant.
# The slope of each line equals the partial regression coefficient.
```
:::

# Model Selection {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## The Problem of Model Complexity {.smaller}

-   How do we decide the complexity of a polynomial: straight line, quadratic, cubic, …?
-   Which variables should we keep or discard when building a multiple regression model?
-   How do we select from candidate models representing different biological processes?

::: callout-important
## Principle of Parsimony

"Models should be pared down until they are minimal and adequate" — Crawley 2007

If two or more models fit the data almost equally well, prefer the simpler model.
:::

## Overfitting with Polynomials {.smaller}

![](images/week07_26_beetle_wing_horn_overfitting.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

The log-likelihood and $R^2$ always increase with more parameters — but this does not mean the model is better!

## The Progression of Polynomial Fits {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Linear fit](images/week07_27_linear_fit_beetle.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Quadratic fit](images/week07_28_quadratic_fit_beetle.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
:::::

## Higher-Order Polynomials and Overfitting {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Degree 5 polynomial](images/week07_29_poly5_fit_beetle.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Degree 10 polynomial](images/week07_30_poly10_fit_beetle.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
:::::

As polynomial degree increases, the model fits the training data ever more closely — but becomes useless for prediction on new data.

## Model Selection Criteria {.smaller}

| Criterion | Description | Selection Rule |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **MS~residuals~** | Mean unexplained variation | Lowest value = best fit |
| **Adjusted R²** | Proportion of variance explained, penalized for \# terms | Larger = better fit |
| **Mallow's Cp** | Comparison to full model | Lowest value, or closest to p |
| **AIC** | Likelihood penalized by number of parameters | Smaller = more parsimonious |
| **BIC** | Like AIC but heavier penalty for complexity | Smaller = more parsimonious |

::: callout-tip
As a rule of thumb, if the difference between two AIC values (ΔAIC) is greater than 2, the lower AIC represents a meaningfully better model.
:::

## Mallow's Cp and All-Subsets Regression {.smaller}

![](images/week07_31_mallows_cp_formula.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(leaps)

# All subsets regression
all_subsets <- regsubsets(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3 + g4, data = RNAseq_Data)
summary(all_subsets)

# Plot Cp, BIC, adjusted R²
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(all_subsets, scale = "Cp")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "bic")
plot(all_subsets, scale = "adjr2")
```

### Key Points

-   **For prediction**: All models with Cp \< p predict about equally well
-   **For explanation**: If numerous models fit equally well, it is difficult to deduce which predictor "explains" the response
-   **General caveat**: "Regression is not causation" — an experiment is needed for causal explanation
:::

## Nested vs. Non-Nested Models {.smaller}

-   **Nested (reduced vs. full)**: One model is a special case of the other — can compare with F-test or likelihood ratio test
-   **Non-nested**: Models contain different sets of variables — compare with AIC or BIC

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Compare nested models with F-test
model_reduced <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2)
model_full    <- lm(y ~ g1 + g2 + g3)
anova(model_reduced, model_full)

# Compare non-nested models with AIC
AIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)
BIC(model_a, model_b, model_c)
```

### Interpretation

-   F-test p \< 0.05 → the fuller model is significantly better
-   Lower AIC/BIC → more parsimonious model
-   BIC penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC
:::

## Stepwise Model Selection in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Start with a full model
full_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ porosity * stiffness * seeding_dens,
                 data = scaffold_data)

# Forward stepwise selection (start from intercept-only)
null_model <- lm(tissue_growth ~ 1, data = scaffold_data)
forward_model <- step(null_model,
                      scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                      direction = "forward", trace = 1)

# Backward elimination (start from full model)
backward_model <- step(full_model, direction = "backward", trace = 1)

# Both directions
both_model <- step(null_model,
                   scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
                   direction = "both", trace = 1)

# Compare final models
AIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)
BIC(forward_model, backward_model, both_model)
```

### Key Points

-   `step()` uses AIC by default; add `k = log(n)` for BIC-based selection
-   Forward selection can miss important combinations
-   Backward elimination can fail when p \> n
-   "Both" direction is generally most robust
-   Stepwise methods can overfit — always validate with cross-validation
:::

# BREAK {background-color="#e74c3c"}

# Statistical Power {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is Power? {.smaller}

Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a **false** null hypothesis (i.e., detecting a real effect when one exists).

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\text{Power} \propto \frac{(\text{Effect Size})(\alpha)(\sqrt{n})}{\sigma}
```
:::

-   Helps interpret failure to reject the null — was the test underpowered?
-   Target: typically **80% power** (β = 0.20)

## Power Overview {.smaller}

![Statistical power and Type II error](images/week09_19_statistical_power_and_type_ii.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Key Components of Power {.smaller}

| Component                  | Description                       |
|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------|
| **Effect Size (ES)**       | Magnitude of difference to detect |
| **Standard Deviation (σ)** | Variability within groups         |
| **Sample Size (n)**        | Number of observations            |
| **Significance Level (α)** | Usually 0.05                      |
| **Power (1 − β)**          | Usually 0.80                      |

![Key questions in power analysis](images/week09_20_key_questions_in_power_analysi.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## Cohen's d {.smaller}

Effect size between two group means expressed in standard deviation units:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{pooled}}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{pooled}}
```
:::

| d   | Interpretation |
|:----|:---------------|
| 0.2 | Small effect   |
| 0.5 | Medium effect  |
| 0.8 | Large effect   |

## Power Analysis in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: power-analysis
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

library(pwr)

# Calculate required sample size for 80% power
sample_size <- pwr.t.test(
  d = 0.5,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

cat("Required n per group:", ceiling(sample_size$n))
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

cat("Required n per group:", ceiling(sample_size$n))
```
:::

## Bootstrap Power Analysis {.smaller}

When parametric assumptions may not hold, use simulation-based power analysis:

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Step 1: Simulate true populations
senior <- rpois(5000, lambda = 10)
fresh  <- rpois(5000, lambda = 12)

# Step 2: Draw samples and test
sample_s <- sample(senior, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
sample_f <- sample(fresh, size = 10, replace = FALSE)
t.test(sample_f, sample_s)

# Step 3: Replicate many times
samps_s <- replicate(n = 100, sample(senior, size = 10))
samps_f <- replicate(n = 100, sample(fresh, size = 10))

# Calculate power
tests <- data.frame(result = numeric(100))
for (i in 1:100) {
  tests$result[i] <- t.test(samps_s[, i], samps_f[, i])$p.value
}
power <- sum(tests$result < 0.05) / 100
cat("Estimated power:", power)
```

### Key Points

-   This approach works for any distribution (Poisson, skewed, etc.)
-   Increase the number of replicates (e.g., 1000+) for stable estimates
-   Can modify sample sizes, effect sizes, or distributions to explore scenarios
:::

## Power Analysis for ANOVA {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(pwr)

# Parameters for one-way ANOVA
effect_size_anova <- 0.25  # Cohen's f (medium)
alpha_anova <- 0.05
power_anova <- 0.8

# Calculate required sample size per group
sample_size_anova <- pwr.anova.test(
  k = 3,                    # Number of groups
  f = effect_size_anova,
  sig.level = alpha_anova,
  power = power_anova
)$n

cat("Sample Size per group for ANOVA:", ceiling(sample_size_anova))
```

### Cohen's f

Cohen's f measures effect size in ANOVA:

| f    | Interpretation |
|:-----|:---------------|
| 0.10 | Small effect   |
| 0.25 | Medium effect  |
| 0.40 | Large effect   |

Cohen's f = √(variance between groups / variance within groups)
:::

## Power Example: Bone Scaffold Experiment {.smaller}

A bioengineering lab needs to determine how many bone scaffolds to test to detect a 15% difference in compressive strength between two scaffold designs.

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Known from pilot data:
# Mean compressive strength: 50 MPa
# Standard deviation: 8 MPa
# Desired detectable difference: 15% = 7.5 MPa

effect_size_d <- 7.5 / 8  # Cohen's d = 0.94

scaffold_power <- pwr.t.test(
  d = effect_size_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = "two.sample"
)

cat("Required scaffolds per group:", ceiling(scaffold_power$n))
cat("\nEffect size (Cohen's d):", round(effect_size_d, 2))
```

### Key Takeaway

-   With a large effect size (d ≈ 0.94), we need relatively few samples
-   If the expected difference were only 5% (3.75 MPa, d ≈ 0.47), sample size would roughly quadruple
-   Always conduct a power analysis **before** running your experiment
:::

## Power for Factorial ANOVA {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(pwr)

# Power for a 2×3 factorial design
# (e.g., 2 scaffold materials × 3 growth factor concentrations)
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,           # Total number of cells (2 × 3)
  f = 0.30,        # Medium-large effect
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)

# For interaction effects specifically:
# Interactions are typically harder to detect
# Use a smaller f value or plan for more samples
pwr.anova.test(
  k = 6,
  f = 0.20,        # Small-medium for interaction
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)
```

### Tip

Interactions typically have **smaller effect sizes** than main effects. Budget extra samples if detecting interactions is important to your study.
:::

## Interactions {.smaller}

An **interaction** means the effect of one variable on the response depends on the state of another variable.

![](images/week07_18_interaction_plots_fertilizer_temperature.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

![](images/week07_13_pesticide_predator_survival_interaction.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## Factorial vs. Nested Designs {.smaller}

**Factorial designs:**

-   All pairwise combinations of factor levels are present
-   Can assess interactions between factors
-   Example: Drug dose × Exercise regimen

**Nested designs:**

-   Hierarchical structure — levels of one factor occur within levels of another
-   No interaction terms (levels are unique to each group)
-   Often contain random effects
-   Example: Cells within wells within plates

## Factorial ANOVA in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

rna_data <- read.table("Stickle_RNAseq.tsv", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")

gene       <- rna_data$Gene100
microbiota <- rna_data$Microbiota
genotype   <- rna_data$Genotype

# Multiplicative model (with interaction)
model_interaction <- aov(gene ~ microbiota * genotype)

# Additive model (no interaction)
model_additive <- aov(gene ~ microbiota + genotype)

summary(model_interaction)
summary(model_additive)
```

### Interpretation

-   If the interaction term is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other
-   If the interaction is not significant, interpret the main effects directly
-   Always check the interaction first before interpreting main effects
:::

# BREAK {background-color="#e74c3c"}

# Random Effects {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Fixed vs. Random Effects {.smaller}

**Fixed effects:**

-   Groups are predetermined, of direct interest, repeatable
-   Examples: medical treatments, predetermined doses, habitat types
-   We want to estimate specific group means

**Random effects:**

-   Groups randomly sampled from a larger population
-   Examples: families, subjects measured repeatedly, blocks, batches
-   **Variance among groups** is of interest, not specific group means

## When to Use Random Effects {.smaller}

-   Nested sampling designs (individuals within populations)
-   Subplots within plots
-   Replicates grouped spatially or temporally (blocks, batches)
-   Related individuals (families, litters)
-   Repeated measures on the same subjects

## Random Effects Hypothesis {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0$$ $$H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0$$

### LaTeX

``` text
H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0
H_A: \sigma^2_\alpha \neq 0
```
:::

We are testing whether the **variance component** for the random effect is zero — i.e., whether there is meaningful variation among the randomly sampled groups.

## Random Effects in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(nlme)

# Random effect model
micro_model_random_effect <- lme(
  fixed  = Gene202 ~ 1,
  random = ~1 | Geno.Micro,
  data   = stickle_micro
)

summary(micro_model_random_effect)
```

### Key Points

-   In R, `lm()` assumes all effects are **fixed**
-   For random effects, use `lme()` from the **nlme** package or `lmer()` from **lme4**
-   The `~1 | group` syntax specifies a random intercept for each level of `group`
:::

## Random Effects: Bioengineering Example {.smaller}

Measuring cell viability across multiple wells within multiple plates within multiple experiments:

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Simulated hierarchical data: cells → wells → plates → experiments
set.seed(42)
n_exp <- 3; n_plate <- 4; n_well <- 6
experiment <- rep(1:n_exp, each = n_plate * n_well)
plate      <- rep(rep(1:n_plate, each = n_well), n_exp)
well       <- rep(1:n_well, n_exp * n_plate)

# Generate data with variance at each level
exp_effect   <- rnorm(n_exp, 0, 5)[experiment]
plate_effect <- rnorm(n_exp * n_plate, 0, 3)[interaction(experiment, plate)]
viability    <- 75 + exp_effect + plate_effect + rnorm(n_exp * n_plate * n_well, 0, 2)

cell_data <- data.frame(
  viability, experiment = factor(experiment),
  plate = factor(plate), well = factor(well)
)

# Fit nested random effects model
library(nlme)
nested_model <- lme(viability ~ 1,
                    random = ~1 | experiment/plate,
                    data = cell_data)
summary(nested_model)

# Extract variance components
VarCorr(nested_model)
```

### Interpreting Variance Components

The output from `VarCorr()` shows:

-   **Experiment variance**: variation between experimental runs
-   **Plate-within-experiment variance**: variation between plates within a run
-   **Residual variance**: well-to-well variation within plates
-   ICC (Intraclass Correlation) = group variance / total variance
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Nested ANOVA {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Nested Design {.smaller}

-   Factors are hierarchical within one another
-   Sources of variance are hierarchical
-   No interaction terms (in completely nested designs)

**Example:** Students within classrooms within schools

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Nested ANOVA using aov
model_nested <- aov(y ~ A + B %in% A, data = mydata)

# Using lme for random nested effects
model_nested_random <- lme(y ~ A, random = ~1 | A/B, data = mydata)

summary(model_nested_random)
```

### Interpretation

-   The `%in%` notation means "B is nested within A"
-   The `~1 | A/B` random effects specification means "random intercepts for B nested within A"
-   Nested designs arise when the levels of one factor are unique to each level of another (e.g., specific cell lines unique to each lab)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Repeated Measures Analysis {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What are Repeated Measures? {.smaller}

Measurements taken on the **same subjects** at multiple:

-   **Time points** (longitudinal studies)
-   **Conditions** (within-subjects design)
-   **Locations** (spatial sampling)

**Advantages:** Controls for individual differences, requires fewer subjects, more statistical power

**Challenge:** Observations are **not independent** — standard ANOVA assumes independence

## Repeated Measures ANOVA {.smaller}

**Sphericity Assumption:**

-   Variances of differences between all pairs of conditions must be equal
-   Often violated in practice

**Mauchly's Test:** Tests the sphericity assumption

-   p \< 0.05 → sphericity is violated → apply correction (Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt)

## Repeated Measures in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: rm-anova-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# Create repeated measures data
set.seed(42)
subject <- factor(rep(1:10, each = 3))
time <- factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), 10))
score <- c(
  rnorm(10, 50, 5),   # Pre
  rnorm(10, 55, 5),   # Mid
  rnorm(10, 62, 5)    # Post
) + rep(rnorm(10, 0, 8), each = 3)  # Subject random effect

rm_data <- data.frame(subject, time, score)

# Repeated measures ANOVA
rm_aov <- aov(score ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data)
summary(rm_aov)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: rm-anova-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Create repeated measures data
set.seed(42)
subject <- factor(rep(1:10, each = 3))
time <- factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), 10))
score <- c(
  rnorm(10, 50, 5),   # Pre
  rnorm(10, 55, 5),   # Mid
  rnorm(10, 62, 5)    # Post
) + rep(rnorm(10, 0, 8), each = 3)  # Subject random effect

rm_data <- data.frame(subject, time, score)

# Repeated measures ANOVA
rm_aov <- aov(score ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data)
summary(rm_aov)
```
:::

## Mixed Models for Repeated Measures {.smaller}

The modern approach uses **linear mixed models**, which are more flexible and handle missing data gracefully:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| message: false

library(nlme)

# Mixed model with random intercept for subject
rm_mixed <- lme(score ~ time, random = ~1 | subject, data = rm_data)
summary(rm_mixed)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(nlme)

# Mixed model with random intercept for subject
rm_mixed <- lme(score ~ time, random = ~1 | subject, data = rm_data)
summary(rm_mixed)
```
:::

## Visualizing Repeated Measures {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: repeated-measures-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Spaghetti plot (individual trajectories)
interaction.plot(rm_data$time, rm_data$subject, rm_data$score,
                 xlab = "Time", ylab = "Score", legend = FALSE,
                 main = "Individual Trajectories", col = "gray")

# Group means with error bars
means <- tapply(rm_data$score, rm_data$time, mean)
sds <- tapply(rm_data$score, rm_data$time, sd)
n <- 10
ses <- sds / sqrt(n)

barplot(means, ylim = c(0, max(means) + max(ses) * 2),
        main = "Group Means ± SE", ylab = "Score")
arrows(x0 = c(0.7, 1.9, 3.1), y0 = means - ses,
       y1 = means + ses, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.1)
```

## Repeated Measures: ggplot Visualization {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: rm-ggplot-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

library(ggplot2)

rm_summary <- rm_data %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarize(mean_score = mean(score), se = sd(score)/sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

p1 <- ggplot(rm_data, aes(x = time, y = score, group = subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = rm_summary, aes(x = time, y = mean_score, group = 1),
            color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = rm_summary, aes(x = time, y = mean_score, group = 1),
             color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(data = rm_summary,
                aes(x = time, y = mean_score, ymin = mean_score - se, ymax = mean_score + se, group = 1),
                width = 0.1, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Spaghetti Plot with Group Mean ± SE",
       x = "Time Point", y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
print(p1)
```

# Week 8: GLMs, Regularization, and Survival Analysis {background-color="#2c3e50"}

# Generalized Linear Models {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is a GLM? {.smaller}

GLMs extend linear models to handle response variables that are not normally distributed. Use when standard linear model assumptions are violated:

-   **Binary response** (e.g., survived/died) → logistic regression
-   **Count response** (e.g., number of mutations) → Poisson regression

**Three components of every GLM:**

1.  **Random component**: probability distribution of the response variable (e.g., binomial, Poisson)
2.  **Systematic component**: linear combination of predictors ($\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \ldots$)
3.  **Link function**: connects the random and systematic components

## GLM Families {.smaller}

| Family   | Link Function | Use For             | Example                  |
|:---------|:--------------|:--------------------|:-------------------------|
| Gaussian | identity      | Continuous response | Standard linear model    |
| Binomial | logit         | Binary outcomes     | Disease presence/absence |
| Poisson  | log           | Count data          | Number of colonies       |
| Gamma    | inverse       | Positive continuous | Reaction times           |

## GLM Assumptions {.smaller}

-   **Independence** of observations
-   No overly **influential observations**
-   **Linearity** between predictors and the link function (not between predictors and raw response)
-   **Appropriate dispersion** (variance matches the assumed distribution)

## GLM in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# General syntax
glm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2, 
    family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
    data = mydata)

# Binomial family for logistic regression
glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial, data = mydata)

# Poisson family for count data
glm(count ~ x1 + x2, family = poisson, data = mydata)
```

### Deviance

-   **Deviance** measures model fit in GLMs (analogous to RSS in linear regression)
-   **Null Deviance**: from model with only intercept
-   **Residual Deviance**: from fitted model
-   Large drop from null to residual deviance → better model fit
:::

## GLM Diagnostics {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Fit a GLM
model <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial, data = mydata)

# Residual deviance plot
plot(predict(model, type = "link"), residuals(model, type = "deviance"),
     xlab = "Linear Predictor", ylab = "Deviance Residuals",
     main = "GLM Deviance Residuals")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

# Influential observations
plot(cooks.distance(model), type = "h",
     main = "Cook's Distance", ylab = "Cook's Distance")

# DHARMa package for simulation-based diagnostics
library(DHARMa)
sim_res <- simulateResiduals(fittedModel = model, n = 1000)
plot(sim_res)  # QQ plot + residual vs predicted
```

### DHARMa Interpretation

The **DHARMa** package creates simulated residuals that work for any GLM family:

-   **QQ plot**: residuals should follow the uniform distribution
-   **Residual vs. predicted**: should show no pattern
-   **Dispersion test**: detects over/underdispersion
-   Works for binomial, Poisson, negative binomial, and zero-inflated models
:::

# Logistic Regression {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is Logistic Regression? {.smaller}

-   Classification algorithm for **binary outcomes** (0/1, yes/no, survived/died)
-   Uses the **logit** link function to map outputs between 0 and 1

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}
```
:::

## The Logistic Function {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: logistic-function-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

curve(1 / (1 + exp(-x)), from = -10, to = 10, col = "blue", lwd = 2,
      ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Linear predictor (β₀ + β₁x)")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray")
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: logistic-function-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

curve(1 / (1 + exp(-x)), from = -10, to = 10, col = "blue", lwd = 2,
      ylab = "Probability", xlab = "Linear predictor (β₀ + β₁x)")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray")
```
:::

## Odds and Log-Odds {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equations

**Odds:** $$\frac{P}{1 - P}$$

**Log-odds (logit):** $$\log\left(\frac{P}{1 - P}\right)$$

**Model equation:** $$\log\left(\frac{P(y=1)}{1 - P(y=1)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\text{Odds} = \frac{P}{1 - P}

\text{Log-odds (logit)} = \log\left(\frac{P}{1 - P}\right)

\text{Model:} \log\left(\frac{P(y=1)}{1 - P(y=1)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
```
:::

## Logistic Regression in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

data(mtcars)
mtcars$am <- factor(mtcars$am)
model <- glm(am ~ mpg, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
summary(model)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

data(mtcars)
mtcars$am <- factor(mtcars$am)
model <- glm(am ~ mpg, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
summary(model)
```
:::

## Interpreting Coefficients {.smaller}

Coefficients are in **log-odds** — exponentiate to get odds ratios:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

exp(coef(model))
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

exp(coef(model))
```
:::

$\exp(\beta_1)$ is the **multiplicative change in odds** for a 1-unit increase in the predictor. For example, if $\exp(\beta_1) = 1.35$, a one-unit increase in mpg multiplies the odds of manual transmission by 1.35 (a 35% increase).

## Bioengineering Example: Predicting Implant Failure {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Simulated implant failure data
set.seed(2026)
n <- 150
implant_data <- data.frame(
  surface_roughness = rnorm(n, 1.5, 0.5),     # μm
  coating_thickness = rnorm(n, 50, 15),         # nm
  load_cycles       = rnorm(n, 5e6, 1e6)       # cycles
)
implant_data$failure <- rbinom(n, 1,
  plogis(-3 + 1.5 * implant_data$surface_roughness -
         0.02 * implant_data$coating_thickness +
         0.0000003 * implant_data$load_cycles))

# Fit logistic regression
implant_glm <- glm(failure ~ surface_roughness + coating_thickness + load_cycles,
                    family = binomial, data = implant_data)
summary(implant_glm)

# Odds ratios
exp(coef(implant_glm))
exp(confint(implant_glm))
```

### Interpretation

-   Higher surface roughness increases odds of failure
-   Thicker coating decreases odds of failure
-   More load cycles increases odds of failure
-   Report odds ratios with 95% CIs for each predictor
:::

## ROC Curve and AUC {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: roc-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(2026)
n <- 150
implant_data <- data.frame(
  surface_roughness = rnorm(n, 1.5, 0.5),
  coating_thickness = rnorm(n, 50, 15),
  load_cycles       = rnorm(n, 5e6, 1e6)
)
implant_data$failure <- rbinom(n, 1,
  plogis(-3 + 1.5 * implant_data$surface_roughness -
         0.02 * implant_data$coating_thickness +
         0.0000003 * implant_data$load_cycles))

implant_glm <- glm(failure ~ surface_roughness + coating_thickness + load_cycles,
                    family = binomial, data = implant_data)

# Manual ROC curve
pred_probs <- predict(implant_glm, type = "response")
thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
tpr <- sapply(thresholds, function(t) {
  pred_class <- ifelse(pred_probs >= t, 1, 0)
  sum(pred_class == 1 & implant_data$failure == 1) / sum(implant_data$failure == 1)
})
fpr <- sapply(thresholds, function(t) {
  pred_class <- ifelse(pred_probs >= t, 1, 0)
  sum(pred_class == 1 & implant_data$failure == 0) / sum(implant_data$failure == 0)
})

plot(fpr, tpr, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "False Positive Rate", ylab = "True Positive Rate",
     main = "ROC Curve — Implant Failure Model")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "gray")

# Approximate AUC using trapezoidal rule
auc <- abs(sum(diff(fpr) * (tpr[-1] + tpr[-length(tpr)])/2))
legend("bottomright", paste("AUC ≈", round(auc, 3)), bty = "n", cex = 1.2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: roc-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Using pROC package for ROC curves
library(pROC)

pred_probs <- predict(implant_glm, type = "response")
roc_obj <- roc(implant_data$failure, pred_probs)

# Plot ROC curve
plot(roc_obj, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     main = "ROC Curve — Implant Failure Model")
cat("AUC:", auc(roc_obj))

# Optimal threshold (Youden's J statistic)
coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))

# Confusion matrix at optimal threshold
optimal_thresh <- coords(roc_obj, "best")$threshold
pred_class <- ifelse(pred_probs >= optimal_thresh, 1, 0)
table(Predicted = pred_class, Actual = implant_data$failure)
```
:::

## Model Evaluation Metrics {.smaller}

| Metric        | Formula                                                     |
|:--------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Accuracy**  | $(TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)$                           |
| **Precision** | $TP / (TP + FP)$                                            |
| **Recall**    | $TP / (TP + FN)$                                            |
| **F1 Score**  | $2 \cdot \frac{Precision \cdot Recall}{Precision + Recall}$ |

## Confusion Matrix {.smaller}

|                     | Predicted Positive  | Predicted Negative  |
|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Actual Positive** | True Positive (TP)  | False Negative (FN) |
| **Actual Negative** | False Positive (FP) | True Negative (TN)  |

# Poisson Regression {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is Poisson Regression? {.smaller}

Models **count data** where the response variable represents the number of times an event occurs:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \ldots + \beta_p x_{ip}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \ldots + \beta_p x_{ip}
```
:::

Assumes Poisson distribution: **Mean = Variance = λ**

## Poisson Regression in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Fit Poisson model
model <- glm(count ~ x1 + x2, family = poisson, data = mydata)

# Check for overdispersion
dispersion <- sum(residuals(model, type = "pearson")^2) / model$df.residual
cat("Dispersion parameter:", dispersion)
# If >> 1, overdispersion is present
```

### Overdispersion Solutions

When variance \> mean (overdispersion):

-   **Quasi-Poisson**: Adjusts standard errors but keeps same coefficients
-   **Negative Binomial**: Adds a parameter for extra-Poisson variation

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Quasi-Poisson
model_qp <- glm(count ~ x1 + x2, family = quasipoisson, data = mydata)

# Negative Binomial
library(MASS)
model_nb <- glm.nb(count ~ x1 + x2, data = mydata)
```
:::

## Poisson Worked Example: Colony Counts {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: poisson-example-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

set.seed(2026)
n <- 120
colony_data <- data.frame(
  coating = factor(rep(c("None", "Fibronectin", "Collagen"), each = 40)),
  seeding = rep(seq(1000, 5000, length.out = 40), 3)
)
colony_data$colonies <- rpois(n, exp(
  1.5 + 0.6 * (colony_data$coating == "Fibronectin") +
  0.9 * (colony_data$coating == "Collagen") +
  0.0003 * colony_data$seeding))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(colonies ~ coating, data = colony_data, col = c("gray80", "lightblue", "salmon"),
        main = "Colony Counts by Coating", ylab = "Number of Colonies")
plot(colony_data$seeding, colony_data$colonies,
     col = c("gray40", "steelblue", "coral")[colony_data$coating],
     pch = 19, cex = 0.8, xlab = "Seeding Density (cells/mL)",
     ylab = "Colony Count", main = "Colonies vs. Seeding Density")
legend("topleft", levels(colony_data$coating),
       col = c("gray40", "steelblue", "coral"), pch = 19, cex = 0.8)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: poisson-example-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Bioengineering Poisson regression: bacterial colony counts
# on tissue culture plates with different surface coatings
set.seed(2026)
n <- 120
colony_data <- data.frame(
  coating = factor(rep(c("None", "Fibronectin", "Collagen"), each = 40)),
  seeding = rep(seq(1000, 5000, length.out = 40), 3)
)
colony_data$colonies <- rpois(n, exp(
  1.5 + 0.6 * (colony_data$coating == "Fibronectin") +
  0.9 * (colony_data$coating == "Collagen") +
  0.0003 * colony_data$seeding))

# Fit Poisson GLM
pois_model <- glm(colonies ~ coating + seeding, family = poisson,
                   data = colony_data)
summary(pois_model)

# Check overdispersion
disp <- sum(residuals(pois_model, type = "pearson")^2) / pois_model$df.residual
cat("Dispersion:", round(disp, 2), "\n")

# If overdispersed, compare models
if (disp > 1.5) {
  qp_model <- glm(colonies ~ coating + seeding, family = quasipoisson,
                   data = colony_data)
  nb_model <- MASS::glm.nb(colonies ~ coating + seeding, data = colony_data)

  cat("Poisson AIC:", AIC(pois_model), "\n")
  cat("Neg Binom AIC:", AIC(nb_model), "\n")
}

# Exponentiate for rate ratios
exp(coef(pois_model))
exp(confint(pois_model))
```
:::

## Poisson vs. Quasi-Poisson vs. Negative Binomial {.smaller}

| Model | Dispersion | Use When | R Function |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Poisson** | φ ≈ 1 | Variance ≈ mean | `glm(..., family = poisson)` |
| **Quasi-Poisson** | φ \> 1 | Mild overdispersion | `glm(..., family = quasipoisson)` |
| **Neg. Binomial** | φ \>\> 1 | Severe overdispersion | `MASS::glm.nb()` |

::: callout-tip
Always check overdispersion first. If the dispersion parameter is close to 1, standard Poisson is fine. If it exceeds \~1.5, consider quasi-Poisson (same coefficients, wider CIs) or negative binomial (different model entirely).
:::

# Regularization Methods {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why Regularization? {.smaller}

Standard linear regression struggles when:

-   **Multicollinearity**: Correlated predictors lead to unstable coefficient estimates
-   **High dimensionality**: More predictors than observations (p \> n)
-   **Overfitting**: Model fits training data too closely, poor generalization

**Solution**: Add a penalty term that **shrinks coefficients toward zero**, trading a small amount of bias for a large reduction in variance.

## Ridge Regression (L2 Penalty) {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\hat{\beta}_{ridge} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2 \right]$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\hat{\beta}_{ridge} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2 \right]
```

### Properties

-   Penalty: $\sum \beta_j^2$ (L2 norm — sum of squared coefficients)
-   Shrinks coefficients toward zero but **never exactly zero**
-   Handles multicollinearity well
-   Closed-form solution: $\hat{\beta}_{ridge} = (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty$
-   As λ → 0: approaches OLS; as λ → ∞: coefficients → 0
:::

## Lasso Regression (L1 Penalty) {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\hat{\beta}_{lasso} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| \right]$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\hat{\beta}_{lasso} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| \right]
```

### Properties

-   Penalty: $\sum |\beta_j|$ (L1 norm — sum of absolute values)
-   Can set coefficients **exactly to zero** → performs variable selection
-   No closed-form solution (requires optimization)
-   Produces **sparse models** — useful when you believe many predictors are irrelevant
:::

## Elastic Net {.smaller}

Combines Ridge and Lasso penalties:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\hat{\beta}_{elastic} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ RSS + \lambda \left( \alpha \sum |\beta_j| + (1-\alpha) \sum \beta_j^2 \right) \right]$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\hat{\beta}_{elastic} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left[ RSS + \lambda \left( \alpha \sum |\beta_j| + (1-\alpha) \sum \beta_j^2 \right) \right]
```
:::

-   α = 0: pure Ridge; α = 1: pure Lasso
-   Variable selection like Lasso + handles correlated features like Ridge
-   Often the best default choice

## Regularization in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(glmnet)

# Ridge regression (alpha = 0)
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)
ridge_model <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0, lambda = ridge_cv$lambda.min)

# Lasso regression (alpha = 1)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
lasso_model <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1, lambda = lasso_cv$lambda.min)

# Elastic net (alpha between 0 and 1)
elastic_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0.5, nfolds = 10)
```

### When to Use

| Method          | Use When                                                |
|:----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| **Ridge**       | Many predictors, most relevant; multicollinearity       |
| **Lasso**       | Feature selection important; many irrelevant predictors |
| **Elastic Net** | Groups of correlated predictors; best of both worlds    |
:::

## Geometric Interpretation {.smaller}

-   **Ridge** constraint region: circle/sphere (smooth boundary) → coefficients shrink continuously
-   **Lasso** constraint region: diamond/polytope (corners at axes) → coefficients can be exactly zero at the corners
-   The intersection of the elliptical RSS contours with the constraint region determines the solution

## Visualizing Regularization Paths {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Fit models across range of lambda values
ridge_path <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0)
lasso_path <- glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1)

# Plot coefficient paths
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ridge_path, xvar = "lambda", main = "Ridge Regression Path")
plot(lasso_path, xvar = "lambda", main = "Lasso Regression Path")
```

### Interpretation

-   Each line represents one coefficient as λ changes
-   Ridge: all coefficients shrink together toward zero
-   Lasso: coefficients drop to exactly zero at different λ values
-   Cross-validation selects the optimal λ
:::

## Regularization Worked Example: Biomaterial Properties {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(glmnet)

# Simulated biomaterial data: 15 material properties predicting biocompatibility
set.seed(42)
n <- 100; p <- 15
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
colnames(X) <- paste0("property_", 1:p)
# Only 4 properties actually matter
y <- 3 * X[,1] - 2 * X[,3] + 1.5 * X[,7] + 0.8 * X[,12] + rnorm(n, 0, 2)

# Step 1: Scale predictors (glmnet does this by default)
# Step 2: Split data
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(n, 0.7 * n)
X_train <- X[train_idx, ]; y_train <- y[train_idx]
X_test  <- X[-train_idx, ]; y_test  <- y[-train_idx]

# Step 3: Fit with cross-validation
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)

# Step 4: Optimal lambda
cat("Lasso lambda.min:", lasso_cv$lambda.min, "\n")
cat("Ridge lambda.min:", ridge_cv$lambda.min, "\n")

# Step 5: Extract coefficients — which properties are selected?
lasso_coefs <- coef(lasso_cv, s = "lambda.min")
print(lasso_coefs)

# Step 6: Compare test set performance
lasso_pred <- predict(lasso_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.min")
ridge_pred <- predict(ridge_cv, X_test, s = "lambda.min")
ols_model  <- lm(y_train ~ X_train)
ols_pred   <- cbind(1, X_test) %*% coef(ols_model)

cat("Test RMSE — Lasso:", sqrt(mean((y_test - lasso_pred)^2)), "\n")
cat("Test RMSE — Ridge:", sqrt(mean((y_test - ridge_pred)^2)), "\n")
cat("Test RMSE — OLS:  ", sqrt(mean((y_test - ols_pred)^2)), "\n")
```

### Visualization

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Plot cross-validation curves
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(lasso_cv, main = "Lasso CV")
plot(ridge_cv, main = "Ridge CV")

# Coefficient path showing variable selection
plot(glmnet(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1), xvar = "lambda",
     main = "Lasso Coefficient Path")
abline(v = log(lasso_cv$lambda.min), lty = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", "lambda.min", lty = 2, col = "red", cex = 0.8)
```
:::

# Splines for Non-Linear Relationships {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What are Splines? {.smaller}

Splines are **piecewise polynomials** that create smooth curves by fitting different polynomial segments between data points.

**Types of Spline Fitting:**

-   **Regression Splines**: Fit using least squares with specified knots
-   **Smoothing Splines**: Balance data fidelity and smoothness automatically
-   **Penalized Splines (P-splines)**: Combine B-spline basis with penalties
-   **Thin Plate Splines**: Extend to multiple dimensions for spatial data

## Splines in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Code

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Natural splines
library(splines)
model_ns <- lm(y ~ ns(x, df = 4), data = mydata)

# Smoothing splines
smooth_fit <- smooth.spline(x, y, cv = TRUE)

# Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)
library(mgcv)
gam_model <- gam(y ~ s(x), data = mydata)

# Thin plate spline for 2D spatial data
model_tp <- gam(z ~ s(x, y, bs = "tp"), data = spatial_data)
```

### Key Points

-   Natural splines constrain the tails to be linear (less extrapolation danger)
-   GAMs use `s()` to automatically select the amount of smoothing
-   Cross-validation (`cv = TRUE`) selects the optimal smoothing parameter
:::

## LOESS Smoothing {.smaller}

LOESS (Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing) fits local polynomial regressions at each point:

![](images/week08_03_loess_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## LOESS Animation {.smaller}

![](images/week08_04_loess_animation.gif){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## LOESS with Different Spans {.smaller}

The span parameter controls the smoothness — smaller values create more flexible fits:

![](images/week08_05_loess_multi_span_animation.gif){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Comparing Fitting Approaches {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: spline-comparison-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

library(splines)
set.seed(42)
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- sin(x) + 0.3 * x + rnorm(100, 0, 0.5)
df <- data.frame(x, y)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Linear
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60", main = "Linear Regression")
m1 <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
lines(x, predict(m1), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

# Polynomial (degree 5)
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60", main = "Polynomial (degree 5)")
m2 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 5), data = df)
lines(x, predict(m2), col = "coral", lwd = 2)

# Natural splines (df = 5)
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60", main = "Natural Splines (df = 5)")
m3 <- lm(y ~ ns(x, df = 5), data = df)
lines(x, predict(m3), col = "forestgreen", lwd = 2)

# GAM with smoothing spline
plot(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "gray60", main = "GAM (Smoothing Spline)")
m4 <- smooth.spline(x, y, cv = TRUE)
lines(m4, col = "purple", lwd = 2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: spline-comparison-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(splines)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# Linear
m1 <- lm(y ~ x)
plot(x, y, pch = 16, col = "gray60", main = "Linear")
lines(x, predict(m1), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)

# Polynomial
m2 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 5))
plot(x, y, pch = 16, col = "gray60", main = "Polynomial (deg 5)")
lines(x, predict(m2), col = "coral", lwd = 2)

# Natural splines
m3 <- lm(y ~ ns(x, df = 5))
plot(x, y, pch = 16, col = "gray60", main = "Natural Splines (df=5)")
lines(x, predict(m3), col = "forestgreen", lwd = 2)

# GAM
m4 <- smooth.spline(x, y, cv = TRUE)
plot(x, y, pch = 16, col = "gray60", main = "GAM")
lines(m4, col = "purple", lwd = 2)
```

### Tradeoffs

| Method          | Flexibility | Extrapolation | Interpretability |
|:----------------|:------------|:--------------|:-----------------|
| Linear          | Low         | Reasonable    | High             |
| Polynomial      | Medium      | Dangerous     | Medium           |
| Natural splines | High        | Linear tails  | Medium           |
| GAM             | High        | Auto-tuned    | Lower            |
:::

# Survival Analysis {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is Survival Analysis? {.smaller}

**Time-to-event analysis** — studying the time until an event occurs:

-   Time until death (clinical trials)
-   Time until device failure (bioengineering)
-   Time until cell division or apoptosis
-   Time until disease recurrence

**Key Features:**

-   **Censoring**: Some subjects haven't experienced the event yet
-   **Non-normal data**: Time data is typically right-skewed
-   **Hazard rates**: Instantaneous risk of the event at any given time

## Censoring in Survival Data {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: censoring-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3

# Visualize censoring concept
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 12), ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), xlab = "Time (months)",
     ylab = "Subject", main = "Survival Data with Censoring", yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = 1:5, labels = paste("Subject", 1:5), las = 1)

# Subject timelines
segments(0, 5, 3, 5, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(3, 5, pch = 4, cex = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)  # Event
segments(0, 4, 8, 4, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(8, 4, pch = 1, cex = 2, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)  # Censored
segments(0, 3, 5, 3, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(5, 3, pch = 4, cex = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)  # Event
segments(0, 2, 10, 2, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(10, 2, pch = 1, cex = 2, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)  # Censored
segments(0, 1, 7, 1, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(7, 1, pch = 4, cex = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)  # Event

legend("topright", c("Event (X)", "Censored (O)"),
       pch = c(4, 1), col = c("red", "darkgreen"), pt.lwd = 2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: censoring-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 12), ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), xlab = "Time (months)",
     ylab = "Subject", main = "Survival Data with Censoring", yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = 1:5, labels = paste("Subject", 1:5), las = 1)

segments(0, 5, 3, 5, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(3, 5, pch = 4, cex = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
segments(0, 4, 8, 4, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
points(8, 4, pch = 1, cex = 2, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
# ... (additional subjects)

legend("topright", c("Event (X)", "Censored (O)"),
       pch = c(4, 1), col = c("red", "darkgreen"), pt.lwd = 2)
```
:::

## The Survival and Hazard Functions {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equations

**Survival function:** $$S(t) = P(T > t) = \text{Probability of surviving past time } t$$

-   $S(0) = 1$ (everyone alive at start)
-   $S(t)$ decreases over time
-   $S(\infty) = 0$ (eventually everyone experiences the event)

**Hazard function:** $$h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{P(t \leq T < t + \Delta t \mid T \geq t)}{\Delta t}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
S(t) = P(T > t)

h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{P(t \leq T < t + \Delta t \mid T \geq t)}{\Delta t}
```
:::

## Kaplan-Meier Estimator {.smaller}

The **product-limit estimator** for the survival function:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \leq t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)$$

Where $d_i$ = events at time $t_i$ and $n_i$ = number at risk before $t_i$

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(survival)
data(lung)

# Fit Kaplan-Meier model
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)

# Plot survival curve
plot(km_fit, xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Survival Probability",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier Survival Curve - Lung Cancer",
     col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, conf.int = TRUE)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "red")
```
:::

## Kaplan-Meier Curves {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

## Log-Rank Test {.smaller}

Tests whether survival curves differ significantly between groups:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Log-rank test comparing survival by sex
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
```
:::

## Cox Proportional Hazards Model {.smaller}

**Semi-parametric model** relating covariates to hazard:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$h(t \mid X) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp(\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \ldots)$$

Where $h_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard and $\exp(\beta)$ is the **hazard ratio** for a 1-unit increase.

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

cox_model <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog, data = lung)
summary(cox_model)
```
:::

## Interpreting Hazard Ratios {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_model), confint(cox_model)))
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Extract hazard ratios with confidence intervals
exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_model), confint(cox_model)))
```

### Interpretation

-   HR = 1: No effect on survival
-   HR \> 1: Increased hazard (worse survival)
-   HR \< 1: Decreased hazard (better survival)
-   Example: HR for sex = 0.59 means females have 41% lower hazard than males
:::

## Checking Proportional Hazards Assumption {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: ph-assumption-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_model)
print(ph_test)
plot(ph_test[2], main = "Schoenfeld Residuals for Sex")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: ph-assumption-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Test proportional hazards assumption
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_model)
print(ph_test)

# Visual check — Schoenfeld residuals should show no trend
plot(ph_test[2], main = "Schoenfeld Residuals for Sex")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)
```
:::

## Bioengineering Example: Scaffold Degradation {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: scaffold-survival-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

library(survival)
set.seed(2026)
n_scaffolds <- 90
scaffold_surv <- data.frame(
  material = factor(rep(c("PLGA", "PCL", "Collagen"), each = 30)),
  time = c(rweibull(30, 2, 14), rweibull(30, 2, 28), rweibull(30, 1.5, 10)),
  event = rbinom(n_scaffolds, 1, 0.85)
)
scaffold_surv$time <- pmax(scaffold_surv$time, 0.5)

km_scaffold <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ material, data = scaffold_surv)
plot(km_scaffold, col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time (weeks)", ylab = "Proportion Intact",
     main = "Scaffold Degradation by Material")
legend("topright", c("Collagen", "PCL", "PLGA"),
       col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"), lwd = 2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: scaffold-survival-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Simulated scaffold degradation data
set.seed(2026)
scaffold_surv <- data.frame(
  material = factor(rep(c("PLGA", "PCL", "Collagen"), each = 30)),
  time = c(rweibull(30, 2, 14),    # PLGA: moderate degradation
           rweibull(30, 2, 28),     # PCL: slow degradation
           rweibull(30, 1.5, 10)),  # Collagen: fast degradation
  event = rbinom(90, 1, 0.85)      # 85% observed degradation
)

# Kaplan-Meier by material
km_scaffold <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ material, data = scaffold_surv)
plot(km_scaffold, col = c("coral", "steelblue", "forestgreen"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time (weeks)", ylab = "Proportion Intact",
     main = "Scaffold Degradation by Material")

# Log-rank test
survdiff(Surv(time, event) ~ material, data = scaffold_surv)

# Cox model: which material degrades fastest?
cox_scaffold <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ material, data = scaffold_surv)
summary(cox_scaffold)
exp(cbind(HR = coef(cox_scaffold), confint(cox_scaffold)))
```

### Interpretation

In this bioengineering context:

-   **Event** = scaffold degradation (loss of structural integrity)
-   **Censored** = scaffold still intact at end of observation period
-   **Hazard ratio** = relative rate of degradation vs. reference material
-   A higher HR means faster degradation
:::

## R Exercise: Logistic Regression {.smaller}

::: callout-tip
## Exercise

A medical researcher wants to predict diabetes using blood glucose and BMI:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Simulated diabetes data
set.seed(123)
n <- 200
glucose <- rnorm(n, 100, 20)
bmi <- rnorm(n, 27, 5)
prob <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(-8 + 0.05 * glucose + 0.1 * bmi)))
diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, prob)
diabetes_data <- data.frame(diabetes, glucose, bmi)
```

Tasks:

1.  Fit logistic regression: `diabetes ~ glucose + bmi`
2.  Interpret the odds ratios (exponentiated coefficients)
3.  Predict probability of diabetes for glucose = 120, BMI = 30
4.  Create a confusion matrix and calculate accuracy
5.  What glucose level gives 50% probability (at mean BMI)?
:::

# Statistical Learning Overview {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## General Steps for Machine Learning {.smaller}

![Machine learning workflow from data collection to deployment](images/week09_22_ml_workflow_steps.pdf){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## What is Statistical Learning? {.smaller}

-   A set of tools for **understanding data** through models
-   **Supervised learning**: predict an outcome from predictors (requires labeled data)
-   **Unsupervised learning**: find patterns without a predefined outcome variable

| Type         | Goal                | Examples                   |
|:-------------|:--------------------|:---------------------------|
| Supervised   | Predict Y from X    | Regression, classification |
| Unsupervised | Find structure in X | Clustering, PCA            |

## Machine Learning Steps {.smaller}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The Overfitting Problem {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Overfitting vs. Underfitting {.smaller}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-caution
## Underfitting

-   Model too simple
-   High bias
-   Misses important patterns
-   Poor performance everywhere
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-warning
## Overfitting

-   Model too complex
-   High variance
-   Memorizes noise
-   Great on training, poor on testing
:::
::::
:::::::

## Bias-Variance Tradeoff {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\text{Test Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Error}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\text{Test Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Error}
```
:::

-   **Bias**: error from incorrect model assumptions (too simple)
-   **Variance**: error from sensitivity to training data (too complex)
-   Goal: balance flexibility with stability

![Bias-variance tradeoff](images/week09_04_bias_variance_tradeoff_visuali.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## In-Class Demo: Overfitting in Action {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: overfit-demo-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

set.seed(1)
x_pop <- runif(1000, 0, 10)
y_pop <- 6 - 0.5 * x_pop + rnorm(1000, sd = 2)

set.seed(0)
idx <- sample(1000, 25)
x_samp <- x_pop[idx]; y_samp <- y_pop[idx]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(x_pop, y_pop, col = "lightblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Linear Model (Appropriate)", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
points(x_samp, y_samp, col = "black", pch = 19)
abline(lm(y_samp ~ x_samp), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 6, b = -0.5, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("True line", "Sample fit"), col = c("blue", "red"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2)

plot(x_pop, y_pop, col = "lightblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "LOESS Model (Overfit)", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
points(x_samp, y_samp, col = "black", pch = 19)
lines(sort(x_samp), predict(loess(y_samp ~ x_samp))[order(x_samp)], col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 6, b = -0.5, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: overfit-demo-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

set.seed(1)
x_pop <- runif(1000, 0, 10)
y_pop <- 6 - 0.5 * x_pop + rnorm(1000, sd = 2)

set.seed(0)
idx <- sample(1000, 25)
x_samp <- x_pop[idx]; y_samp <- y_pop[idx]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Linear model: appropriate fit
plot(x_pop, y_pop, col = "lightblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "Linear Model (Appropriate)", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
points(x_samp, y_samp, col = "black", pch = 19)
abline(lm(y_samp ~ x_samp), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 6, b = -0.5, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

# LOESS: overfitting
plot(x_pop, y_pop, col = "lightblue", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     main = "LOESS Model (Overfit)", xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
points(x_samp, y_samp, col = "black", pch = 19)
lines(sort(x_samp), predict(loess(y_samp ~ x_samp))[order(x_samp)],
      col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(a = 6, b = -0.5, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```
:::

# Cross-Validation {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is Cross-Validation? {.smaller}

-   Assess model performance on **unseen data**
-   Reduce overfitting by testing generalization
-   Compare different models objectively

![](images/week09_06_crossvalidation1.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## Training vs Testing Data {.smaller}

![](images/week09_07_crossvalidation2.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Overfitting Problem {.smaller}

![](images/week09_08_crossvalidation3.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## K-Fold CV Concept {.smaller}

**Process:**

1.  Split data into k folds
2.  Train on k − 1 folds
3.  Test on remaining fold
4.  Repeat k times
5.  Average results

![](images/week09_09_crossvalidation4.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## K-Fold Cross-Validation Illustration {.smaller}

![](images/week09_10_crossvalidation5.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## CV Results Comparison {.smaller}

![](images/week09_11_crossvalidation6.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## Model Selection with CV {.smaller}

![](images/week09_12_crossvalidation7.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## CV Summary {.smaller}

![](images/week09_13_crossvalidation8.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

## K-Fold Cross-Validation in R {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: cv-example
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

library(boot)

set.seed(123)
n <- 100
x <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

model <- glm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = data)
cv_result <- cv.glm(data, model, K = 10)
cat("10-fold CV MSE:", round(cv_result$delta[1], 4))
```

### Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(boot)

set.seed(123)
n <- 100
x <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

model <- glm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = data)
cv_result <- cv.glm(data, model, K = 10)
cat("10-fold CV MSE:", round(cv_result$delta[1], 4))
```
:::

## Choosing K {.smaller}

| K      | Description           | Properties                       |
|:-------|:----------------------|:---------------------------------|
| K = 5  | 5-fold CV             | Good balance, common choice      |
| K = 10 | 10-fold CV            | Most popular default             |
| K = n  | Leave-one-out (LOOCV) | Maximum training data, expensive |

## CV for Polynomial Degree Selection {.smaller}

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: cv-poly-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(42)
n <- 80
x <- runif(n, 0, 6)
y <- 2 + 3*x - 0.5*x^2 + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)
df <- data.frame(x, y)

cv_errors <- numeric(10)
for (d in 1:10) {
  cv_err <- 0
  for (i in 1:n) {
    fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = df[-i, ])
    pred <- predict(fit, df[i, , drop = FALSE])
    cv_err <- cv_err + (df$y[i] - pred)^2
  }
  cv_errors[d] <- cv_err / n
}

plot(1:10, cv_errors, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Polynomial Degree", ylab = "LOOCV Error (MSE)",
     main = "Cross-Validation for Model Selection")
abline(v = which.min(cv_errors), lty = 2, col = "red")
legend("topright", paste("Optimal degree =", which.min(cv_errors)),
       col = "red", lty = 2, bty = "n")
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: cv-poly-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# LOOCV to select optimal polynomial degree
set.seed(42)
n <- 80
x <- runif(n, 0, 6)
y <- 2 + 3*x - 0.5*x^2 + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)
df <- data.frame(x, y)

cv_errors <- numeric(10)
for (d in 1:10) {
  cv_err <- 0
  for (i in 1:n) {
    fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = df[-i, ])
    pred <- predict(fit, df[i, , drop = FALSE])
    cv_err <- cv_err + (df$y[i] - pred)^2
  }
  cv_errors[d] <- cv_err / n
}

# Plot CV error vs. complexity
plot(1:10, cv_errors, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "Polynomial Degree", ylab = "LOOCV MSE",
     main = "Cross-Validation for Model Selection")
abline(v = which.min(cv_errors), lty = 2, col = "red")

# The "elbow" shows where adding complexity stops helping
cat("Optimal degree:", which.min(cv_errors))
```

### Key Insight

-   CV error initially decreases as model becomes more flexible
-   After the optimal point, overfitting causes CV error to **increase**
-   This "elbow" identifies the best bias-variance tradeoff
-   Connects directly to model selection from Week 7
:::
